content:
Hi all — I've been building FORMA, a natural language to Lean 4 translation system with self-iterating verification: when generated code fails lake build, the error is automatically fed back to the LLM for repair, iterating up to 6 times until the proof compiles.

Demo: forma-three-beige.vercel.app

Note: the self-iterating verification feature requires a local server to be running, so it may not be available at all times in the current beta. Basic NL-to-Lean translation will still work. We plan to fully publish once translation accuracy
reaches a satisfactory threshold.

A question I've been thinking about: beyond prompt engineering, what are the most promising approaches for training agents to improve NL-to-formal translation quality? Specifically:

  • Fine-tuning on Mathlib proof corpora?
  • Reinforcement learning from lake build feedback?
  • Synthetic data generation from existing proofs?

This is part of a broader project at Chaos Butterfly (chaosbutterfly.ai) — we're building formal verification infrastructure for AI systems, with FORMA as one of the core tools.

Would love to hear thoughts from anyone working in this space.

The kind-of-standard approach is to SFT on the next quality data you can get (either natural or synthetic), then leverage the verifier to perform RL.
Even SFT alone proved to give significant performance boost to LLMs, better than what prompt engineer achieves.
One important aspect to notice is that LEAN won't check the correctness if the statement (that it does match the natural language description), so there should be careful handling of that part.

Thank you, this is really helpful! On the RL point: FORMA currently uses an iterative
loop where lake build errors are fed back to the LLM for correction, which is a lightweight version of this idea without actual training. The logical next step would be collecting these (NL, Lean, success/fail) triples as training data for SFT.
Your point about statement correctness is the harder problem — Lean verifies proof validity but not semantic faithfulness to the original NL description. We handle this partially through prompt design, but it's not robust.
Do you know of any work that specifically addresses the statement alignment problem?
